title: Two Ways to Build It: The Architectural Bets Compared

know: The map of bets, each with a dated fact for both companies or the words 'not public': license and money-holding (a credit institution with branches against e-money institutions, state licenses, partner banks and, in business since 28 May 2026, a Georgia limited-purpose acquiring bank of Stripe's own); acquiring (84% full-stack, with 14 countries and regions listed as having an Adyen acquiring connection, against own entities in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific and other named acquirers, most of them banks, elsewhere); build or buy (two acquisitions, both in 2026, against at least ten since 2020); one platform or a suite; first customers and default pricing (Interchange++ with tiers against a published blended rate, with interchange-plus listed among Stripe's custom options); hosting (data centers whose servers Adyen manages itself, with six regions named and no cities or operators, against AWS by Stripe's 2023 statement, with no AWS region named); billing and revenue products (no billing product and no first-party tax engine of Adyen's own found until Orb, and Adyen's statement that it is not a merchant of record, against Billing since 2018, plus tax, revenue recognition and a merchant-of-record product for digital goods); platforms.

Which of these are differences of kind, which of default, sequence or degree, and which the public record cannot decide: Stripe's reasons for partner banks, the volume share of each acquirer, the acquiring entity per country at Adyen, realized prices, any independent measure of approval rates.

Why 'one platform against a suite' compares two different things: a statement about Adyen's engineering and operations with a statement about Stripe's packaging; Stripe has published nothing about a single code base.

The integrator-visible consequences the earlier parts documented: a payment a client can read again against a reference plus events; idempotency keys kept at least 24 hours against 7 to 14 days; a version set per account or header against one written in every URL; published rate limits against none published for payments; funds made available per transaction against a pre-financed sales-day payout.
believe: The choice between the two is made bet by bet and country by country; neither 'the bank against the API' nor 'enterprises against startups' survives the dated record.
A stated reason for a difference is an inference unless the company gave it, and should be labeled so.
can_do: For a described business, list which documented differences bear on its decision, which do not, and what it must ask each provider because the record is silent.
Classify any claimed Stripe and Adyen difference as one of kind, one of degree or default, or one that cannot be decided from public sources, with a dated fact for each side.
Fill in the provider comparison card for a business that runs both.

audience.who: Engineers and architects new to payments who have read the mechanism chapters of Parts I to VIII and the two cases, and who must choose between Stripe and Adyen, combine them, or explain to a colleague why a slogan about them is wrong.
already_knows: What an API, a webhook, an idempotency key, a region and a data center are.

From earlier chapters: acquirer, e-money institution, partner bank, payment facilitator, safeguarding, interchange, payout, merchant of record; each is glossed again in one clause where first used here.

The two records as the cases left them: Stripe built the interface first and assembled the regulated layer afterward as a non-bank; Adyen built the license and the platform first and bought adjacent software in 2026.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two businesses the chapter does not describe, the reader says which documented differences matter to each and avoids deciding by company size alone.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two companies ask the same question. A: thirty engineers, sells software subscriptions online in twenty countries, bills partly by usage, has no finance team that audits card costs. B: a retailer with four hundred stores in eight European countries, billing done in its ERP, a treasury team that reconciles cost by card type. Using only this chapter: for each, which documented differences between Stripe and Adyen bear on the choice, which do not, and what can neither record tell them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A: Stripe's own subscription engine (since 2018), usage metering and Metronome, tax and revenue-recognition products, a published blended rate, self-serve activation and a payment object it can read again all bear on the choice; Adyen had no billing product of its own until it bought Orb in July 2026, which it described in June 2026 as run under an incubator model and says it is integrating. The bank-or-not difference matters little to A. B: Adyen's reported in-person volume (€310.9 billion in 2025, 22% of its volume) and terminal estate, Interchange++ pricing with volume tiers as the default, acquiring across the EEA under one banking license, and a sales-day payout that Adyen pre-finances bear on the choice; the billing difference does not. Stripe offers in-person payments and interchange-plus pricing on request but publishes no in-person volume. Neither record gives realized prices, an independent measure of approval rates, or volume per acquirer; both companies must be asked. Size alone decides nothing: each now sells to the other's first customers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a list of claimed differences, the reader classifies each as of kind, of degree or default, or undecidable, with one dated fact per company.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter, classify each statement as a difference of kind that holds in November 2026, a difference of degree or default, or not decidable from the public record, and give one dated fact for each company: (1) 'Adyen is a bank and Stripe is not.' (2) 'Adyen acquires itself and Stripe uses sponsors.' (3) 'Adyen builds and Stripe buys.' (4) 'Adyen runs its own data centers and Stripe runs on a public cloud.' (5) 'Stripe chose partner banks to enter markets faster.'
acceptance_criteria.expected: (1) Kind: Adyen N.V. is a credit institution licensed in 2017, with a US branch (2021) and UK authorization (2023); Stripe states 'Stripe is not a bank' (2026) and operates e-money institutions and state money-transmitter licenses. (2) Degree: Adyen reports 84% full-stack volume (2025), lists 14 countries and regions with an Adyen acquiring connection (n.d., accessed 2026) and names banking partners where it has no license; Stripe's disclosure (accessed 2026) names its own entities as acquirer in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific, other named acquirers, most of them banks, in North America and some Asian markets, and its own Georgia bank, in business since 28 May 2026, in the US. (3) Degree since 2026: Adyen closed two acquisitions on 1 July 2026, the only ones its history page lists; Stripe has named at least ten since 2020. (4) Kind: Adyen says most of its capital expenditure is data centers (2025) and names six data-center regions; Stripe said 'We couldn't run without AWS' (2023). (5) Not decidable: Stripe has published no reason; the statement is an inference and the chapter labels it so.

acceptance_criteria.statement: In the comparison map, every Stripe cell and every Adyen cell is a documented fact with its year or the words 'Not public', and every reason offered for a difference is introduced as inference.
A reader of the introduction alone can predict the bets the chapter compares, in order, and how it sorts them.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: which bets will this chapter compare, in what order, and into what kinds will it sort the differences?
acceptance_criteria.expected: License and money-holding; acquiring and connectivity; build or buy; one platform or a suite; first customers, the API model and pricing; hosting; billing and revenue products; platforms. Sorted into differences of kind that still hold, differences of degree or default that narrowed in 2025 and 2026, and questions the public record cannot decide, each with what it means for a customer.

thesis.question: On which architectural bets do Stripe and Adyen demonstrably differ in November 2026, and what should a customer choosing or combining them do with each difference?
thesis.claim: Two of the bets are differences of kind that both records document: who holds the money (a licensed bank against e-money institutions with partner banks) and who runs the machines (own data-center capacity against AWS). The rest (acquiring, build or buy, first customers and pricing, billing products, the API model) are differences of default, sequence or degree that narrowed in 2025 and 2026, and 'one platform against a suite' sets an engineering statement beside a packaging statement. A customer should therefore treat the two kinds differently: for a difference of kind, establish per country which entity will hold its funds and what it depends on; for a difference of degree or default, compare the default it will live with and ask for the alternative; and decide on neither company's slogan.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the two companies embody opposite architectures that follow from their customers, 'Stripe for startups, Adyen for enterprises', so that company size settles the choice; and the engineer's version of it, that Adyen owns the stack and Stripe rents it, so that the comparison is one row long.
thesis.so_what: The decision becomes a card with rows and dates instead of a preference. A business that runs both, as Larkfield (fictional) does, knows which differences it must absorb in its own payment service (two fee models, two payout timings, two sets of regulated entities, two webhook contracts) and which it can ignore; a business choosing one knows which questions to put to the sales team because the public record does not answer them.
thesis.how_why: The 'Where They Differ' tables of Parts I to VIII, gathered, sort themselves by evidence. Where both companies have documented a structural fact, the difference is of kind: Adyen's banking licenses and Stripe's 'not a bank'; Adyen's data-center capital expenditure and Stripe's statement on AWS (2023; a 2024 AWS post co-written by Stripe engineers is consistent with it). Where the facts are the same in type and differ in amount, order or default, it is of degree: Stripe's own entities acquire in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific while Adyen is full-stack for 84% of volume; Stripe built Billing in 2018 and bought Metronome in 2026 while Adyen bought Orb in 2026; Stripe's default is a published blended rate with interchange-plus among its custom options, while Adyen's default is Interchange++ with volume tiers; each began with one kind of customer and now sells to the other's. Where one company has published nothing (Stripe's reasons for partner banks, its sponsor shares, its code structure; Adyen's integration dates and a complete list of its acquiring entities per country; either one's realized prices), the chapter says 'not public' and gives any reason only as labeled inference. The clearest integrator-facing differences are defaults. That they fit each company's first customers is the author's inference, and it is a statement about where the defaults came from, not about which customer should choose which company today: a self-serve, re-readable API with published limits on one side; one with methods and features enabled on request, explicit versions, longer retry windows and pre-financed payouts on the other.

supporting_claims.claim: Sorted by the evidence behind them, the differences between Stripe and Adyen fall into three kinds: differences of kind, where both companies document a structural fact; differences of default, sequence or degree, where the facts are of the same type and differ in amount, order or default; and questions the public record cannot decide, where any reason offered is an inference.

Two bets are differences of kind that hold in November 2026: who holds the money (one licensed bank with two branches against e-money institutions, state licenses and partner banks) and who runs the machines (own infrastructure in data centers against AWS).

Acquiring, build or buy, first customers with the pricing and API defaults they left, billing and revenue products, and platform loss bearing are differences of default, sequence or degree, and each narrowed in 2025 and 2026; 'one platform against a suite' is not a like-for-like row, because it sets a statement about Adyen's operation beside a statement about Stripe's packaging.

On several points one company or both have published nothing (Stripe's reasons for partner banks, volume per acquirer, Adyen's acquiring entity per country, realized prices, an independent measure of approval rates); there the chapter says 'not public' and offers reasons only as labeled inference.

A customer therefore decides bet by bet and country by country: for a difference of kind it establishes which entity holds its funds and what the provider depends on; for a difference of degree or default it compares the default it will live with and asks for the alternative; a business on both providers, as Larkfield (fictional) is, knows which differences its own payment service must absorb.

role.contribution: Turns the two cases and the book's 'Where They Differ' tables into one argued map, and is the page on which the journal's provisional reading of the two companies is confirmed in part and corrected in part.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene, sorting, then the bets: the decision and the sorting rule come before anything is sorted
the eight bets: from the regulated base (money, acquiring) through how products are made and packaged, to the customer-facing defaults, the machines, and the two product areas built on top

flow.rationale: The reader meets the decision first, then the rule for sorting evidence, because every bet section applies that rule. The bets run in the order the journal entry fixes: the regulated layer first (who holds the money, who acquires), since the slogans are about it; then how each company makes and packages products (build or buy, platform or suite); then the customers and the defaults they left in price and API; then hosting; then the two product areas, billing and platforms, which depend on the earlier bets (the license returns in platforms, build-or-buy in billing). The map comes after the bets because it summarizes cells the reader has already seen argued; put first, its 'kind' column would be assertion. The decision aid comes last because it uses only the documented cells of the map. Moving hosting next to money-holding would pair the two differences of kind but break the order the introduction promises and separate the API defaults from the customers that explain them.

hook.content: Two sentences are said in most provider evaluations: 'Stripe is for startups, Adyen is for enterprises' and 'Adyen owns the stack, Stripe rents it.' Against them stand two dated lines from the companies themselves: Stripe's acquirer disclosure (accessed November 2026) says for the European Economic Area 'Payment Method Acquirer is Stripe Technology Europe, Ltd.', and Adyen's third-quarter 2026 update says its Platforms offering 'allows us to provide payments and financial products to smaller merchants, which will be a key driver of future growth'.

bridge.from_reader_world: An engineer who has read forty-one 'Where They Differ' tables and two cases holds about 250 rows of difference and no way to tell which of them should decide a choice of provider.
bridge.to_topic: Sorted by the evidence behind each row, the differences reduce to eight bets of three kinds, and the kind says what a customer should do with each.

thesis_statement.text: Two bets are differences of kind that both records document: who holds the money and who runs the machines. The others are differences of default, sequence or degree that narrowed in 2025 and 2026, 'one platform against a suite' compares an engineering statement with a packaging statement, and some questions the public record cannot decide. A customer treats each kind differently and decides on neither company's slogan.

evidence.what: The sorting rule in the journal entry's thesis (how_why): 'Where both companies have documented a structural fact, the difference is of kind ... Where the facts are the same in type and differ in amount, order or default, it is of degree ... Where one company has published nothing ... the chapter says not public'.

sections.heading: Who Holds the Money: A Bank and a Non-Bank
sections.controlling_idea: Adyen is one licensed bank with two branches and Stripe is a non-bank that holds funds through e-money institutions, state licenses and partner banks; this is a difference of kind that both document, and it shows in where balances sit, who can pay out before funds arrive and who lends.

advances_thesis.how: Establishes the first difference of kind and what a customer must find out per country because of it.

transition_in.introduces: The first bet to which it is applied: the license and who holds the money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen N.V. is a credit institution, a bank, with a US federal branch and a UK branch; Stripe states that it is not a bank and holds permissions function by function: e-money institutions in Ireland and the United Kingdom, state money-transmitter licenses in the United States, and a partner bank for stored balances.

evidence.what: [[licences-and-safeguarding]] table rows 'License in the EEA', 'in the UK', 'in the US'; [[case-adyen]]: 'Adyen N.V. is authorised as a credit Institution under the supervision of Dutch Central Bank' (https://www.adyen.com/licenses/emea, n.d., accessed November 2026; re-fetched), banking license 2017, US branch 2021, UK authorization 2023. [[case-stripe]]: 'Stripe is not a bank. Checking accounts are provided exclusively by Fifth Third Bank, National Association, Member FDIC.' (https://docs.stripe.com/treasury.md, n.d., accessed November 2026; re-fetched); Stripe Technology Europe an e-money institution (Central Bank of Ireland, page of April 2019), Stripe Payments UK an e-money institution (FCA, page of January 2017), Stripe Payments Company 'a U.S. state-licensed money transmitter' (terms updated November 2025).
evidence.shows: Both companies document a structural fact, so the difference is of kind.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The license shows in three places a customer can see: where balances sit, whether a standard payout can be paid before the network has paid, and who the lender is behind financial products.

evidence.what: [[licences-and-safeguarding]] rows 'Where customer funds sit' and 'Paying out before funds arrive': Stripe, safeguarding accounts at unnamed credit institutions (EU, UK; FAQ 2024); Adyen, business-account deposits at Adyen N.V. under the Dutch deposit guarantee, balances waiting for payout Not public. [[clearing-and-settlement]] and ruling 18: Adyen's Sales Day Payout terms (17 June 2024, https://www.adyen.com/legal/sales-day-payout-terms-of-service; re-fetched) pay 'irrespective of whether the funds are actually received by Adyen from the Acquirer or Scheme Owner', 'Prefinancing is capped at 30 days'; Stripe documents paying ahead only for Instant Payouts. [[case-adyen]]: the annual report calls paying only after funds are received the 'default setup', which the case could not reconcile. [[embedded-finance]] row 'License behind the products': Stripe's partner banks and outside lenders; 'Adyen is the lender'.
evidence.shows: Turns the license from a legal fact into three behaviors an integrator meets.

transition_in.introduces: What the form changes that a customer can observe.

evidence.what: [[licences-and-safeguarding]] and ruling 33; [[case-stripe]]: Georgia Department of Banking and Finance bulletin of May 2026 (approved 30 June 2025, in business since 28 May 2026); Stripe MALPB terms (https://stripe.com/legal/stripe-malpb-acquirer-terms, last updated 28 May 2026; re-fetched): 'a Georgia Merchant Acquirer Limited Purpose Bank'; such banks 'may not solicit or accept deposits from the general public' (ICBA news item, 8 July 2025, secondary source); OCC 'preliminary conditional approval' for Bridge National Trust Bank, 12 February 2026, no final approval found.

sections.heading: Who Acquires: A Difference of Degree, Country by Country
sections.controlling_idea: Both companies acquire card payments under their own licenses in some markets and rely on others elsewhere; they differ in where, and in what each publishes about it.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the most repeated difference is one of degree, and that the slogan fails for Europe.

transition_in.introduces: The bet most often mistaken for one: who acquires.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe's disclosure names its own entities as acquirer in the EEA, the United Kingdom, Brazil and much of Asia-Pacific and other named acquirers elsewhere, among them its own Georgia bank in the United States; Adyen reports 84% of 2025 volume as full-stack, lists 14 countries and regions with an Adyen acquiring connection, names a licensed entity for some markets, and publishes no list of acquiring entities per country.

evidence.what: [[acquiring-and-network-connectivity]] rows 'Acquirer of record' and 'Where a partner bank stands in'; [[journey-of-a-payment]] row 'Where its own acquiring stops'; rulings 11, 27, 33. Stripe acquirer disclosure (https://stripe.com/legal/acquirer-disclosure, n.d., accessed 17 November 2026; re-fetched): 'Stripe, LLC is a Payment Facilitator of' Cross River Bank, Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, Fifth Third Bank, Pathward N.A., PNC Bank N.A. and Stripe MALPB; named acquirers in Canada, Japan (card companies), Thailand, India ('Payment Aggregator'), the United Arab Emirates ('Independent Sales Organization'); Mexico both acquirer and facilitator. Adyen Annual Report 2025: 'Of processed volumes, 84% were full-stack volumes'; concentration risk 'primarily at banking partners in locations where there are no own direct acquiring licenses'. paragraphs.controlling_idea: So 'Adyen acquires itself and Stripe uses sponsors' is wrong for Europe and roughly right for the United States; what differs most is what each publishes, Stripe the legal entity per country and Adyen the size of its own share, and Adyen's own acquiring is a condition for some of its features.

advances_thesis.how: Shows a difference of sequence and dates the point at which it narrowed.

sections.heading: One Platform or a Suite: Two Statements About Different Things
sections.controlling_idea: 'Single platform' is Adyen's statement about how it operates and 'suite' is Stripe's way of packaging and selling; they are not two answers to one question, and seen from the integrator's side they nearly cross.

evidence.shows: Shows the two statements are about different things.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the interface the two nearly cross: Adyen's platform is integrated through several API families with their own versions, Stripe's suite through one object model, and Stripe sells products that sit over other providers' processing while Adyen argues for carrying the payment itself.

evidence.what: INFERENCE block, from [[payment-routing-and-orchestration]]: holding the layer above the payment (checkout, billing, fraud, vault) may be worth more to Stripe than carrying every authorization; Adyen's argument rests on carrying the payment. Neither has said this.

transition_in.introduces: How they look from the integrator's side.

[[case-adyen]]: 'Single platform is not a single process: 3,000 services'.

sections.heading: Who Runs the Machines: Own Infrastructure and a Public Cloud
sections.controlling_idea: Adyen runs its own infrastructure in data centers and reports what it costs; Stripe runs on AWS by its own statement; this is the second difference of kind, and an integrator meets it as a region setting on one side and none on the other.

advances_thesis.how: Establishes the second difference of kind and what it does and does not let a customer plan on.

transition_in.carries_over: Defaults that a customer can ask to change.
transition_in.introduces: A second difference of kind, which no customer can ask to change: who runs the machines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen manages its own infrastructure in data centers, names six regions and reports data centers as the majority of its capital expenditure; Stripe said in 2023 that it could not run without AWS and names no AWS region.

evidence.what: [[payment-multi-region-and-data-residency]] rows 'Hosting' and 'Where the data centers are'; [[case-adyen]]: 'We manage our own infrastructure in several data centers around the world' (2021 post; evidence age 5 years); capital expenditure 'EUR 116.8 million and 5% of net revenues' in 2025, 'The majority of our CapEx is related to our data centers'; data centers 'in Europe, the United States, India, Singapore, Japan and Australia' and 'We administer and manage all our own servers' (https://www.adyen.com/infrastructure, n.d., accessed November 2026; re-fetched); no cities or operators; 'data center partners' in the annual report. [[case-stripe]]: 'Stripe has long relied on AWS to provide the core compute infrastructure on which Stripe is built'; 'We couldn't run without AWS—and we wouldn't want to' (release of 23 January 2023, https://stripe.com/newsroom/news/amazon-and-stripe; re-fetched; evidence age almost 4 years; an October 2024 AWS post co-written by Stripe staff is consistent).
evidence.shows: Both document a structural fact: a difference of kind. [[payment-multi-region-and-data-residency]] calls it 'The clearest documented architectural difference between the two'.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An integrator meets the difference in three places: region is a setting in Adyen's integration and absent from Stripe's; Adyen states that payments are stored in Europe and Stripe states no storage location; and capacity is bought ahead on one side and rented on the other, with Adyen documenting a peak freeze and load-balancer failover in general terms.

evidence.what: [[payment-multi-region-and-data-residency]] rows 'Regions an integrator can name', 'European data', 'Several data centers at once': five live regions for online payments (EU, US, AU, NEA, IN) against one base URL; payments 'stored in Europe and our isolated India environment'; neither promises data stays in the EU; 'active/active', load balancers 'manage the failover to the other data centers' (https://docs.adyen.com/industries/peak-season, n.d.; re-fetched), no topology or timings; for Stripe not found. [[payment-peak-load]] row 'How capacity is obtained': utilization 'generally less than 30%', investment pulled forward 'to secure compute and storage availability' (2026); Stripe shards split in surges (2024); freeze around named peak days documented by Adyen only.
evidence.shows: Shows where a difference in hosting reaches the integrator.

evidence.what: INFERENCE block, from [[payment-peak-load]] and [[case-adyen]]: provisioning time on one side, purchase lead time on the other; 'single platform' read as a statement about cost. Adyen's own stated reasons for not using a public cloud are 'part historical, part legal, and part technical' (2021); Stripe gives none beyond 'we wouldn't want to'.
evidence.shows: Separates the documented reasons from the author's reading.

transition_in.introduces: Where an integrator meets it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Neither company publishes a failover design, timings or the cities of its data centers, and their availability figures cannot rank them, so a customer records the hosting dependency of each provider, treats residency as a setting to check on Adyen and a contract question on Stripe, and rests no plan on either provider's failover.

evidence.what: [[payment-reliability-and-availability]] rows 'Reported figures' and 'Contractual commitment': 'Neither publishes a consistent yearly series, so the figures cannot rank the two'; Adyen 99.9% per quarter by 'commercially reasonable efforts' (terms of November 2023), none found for Stripe; 'No plan of yours can rest on either provider's failover'. [[case-stripe]] and [[case-adyen]] 'Where the Evidence Stops': AWS regions; cities, operators, how failover works.

sections.heading: Billing and Revenue Products: Built from 2018, Bought in 2026

advances_thesis.how: Shows the widest product difference as one of sequence that began to narrow in 2026 and has not yet changed an integration.

Adyen's own stated reason for buying Orb is in [[case-adyen]]; neither company states the reasoning about customers.

sections.heading: Platforms: Who Stands Behind the Seller
sections.controlling_idea: Both companies sell a platform product with balances per seller; they differ in how a seller is modeled, in who bears a seller's losses by default and in whether that assignment can change, and the license bet returns in the financial products built on top.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the platform bet as a difference of default, with the loss-bearing option documented on both sides.

transition_in.carries_over: Billing as a difference of sequence.
transition_in.introduces: The last bet, also one of default: platforms and who bears a seller's loss.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe expresses the merchant per payment, by charge type, on one account per seller; Adyen expresses it by integration model and separates a seller into a legal entity, an account holder, a balance account and a transfer instrument, and it decides refunds and chargebacks by an instruction on each payment where Stripe decides by the kind of charge.

evidence.what: [[platform-payment-models]] rows 'How the merchant is expressed', 'What represents a seller', 'Where a chargeback is booked'; [[splits-balances-and-platform-payouts]] rows 'How a payment is divided' and 'A split that cannot be booked as sent' (a Stripe transfer fails with an error; Adyen books to the liable balance account without an error). [[case-stripe]]: Connect since October 2012, 'More than 18,000 platforms' (September 2026). [[case-adyen]]: Platforms net revenue EUR 263.8 million in 2025.
evidence.shows: Same product type, different modeling: the base for the default that follows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On who bears a seller's losses the two are closer than commonly said: Stripe offers itself as loss bearer as a setting per account that cannot be changed later, and Adyen's default is the platform's own liable account, with Adyen bearing the loss under Managed Risk, a pilot with limited availability.

evidence.what: [[platform-payment-models]] rows 'Who stands behind a seller's negative balance', 'Can the assignment change?', 'Recovery'; ruling 41. Stripe: losses_collector, 'You can't update their values later' (https://docs.stripe.com/connect/accounts-v2/connected-account-configuration, n.d.; re-fetched). Adyen: 'Adyen allows negative balances for up to 30 days'; Managed Risk 'is in pilot phase', Adyen will 'assume the responsibility for negative balances', written off after 180 days (https://docs.adyen.com/platforms/managed-risk, n.d., accessed November 2026; re-fetched). [[embedded-finance]]: Stripe's reach per country depends on a partner, Adyen's on where its license extends; accounts for a platform's sellers generally available at neither.
evidence.shows: A provider that bears seller losses is documented on both sides, at different release stages: a difference of default.

evidence.what: INFERENCE block (the author's): Stripe's setting suits a platform with no risk function of its own, which matches the software companies it started with; Adyen's default assumes a platform able to carry and manage its sellers' risk. Neither company says so.
evidence.shows: Reason labeled as the author's own.

transition_in.introduces: Who bears the seller's loss, where the two are closer than assumed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen's platform price list and both companies' underwriting criteria are not public, so a platform decides who bears seller losses before it creates the first Stripe account, sends and stores the chargeback instruction on every Adyen payment, and asks each provider for the release stage of every financial product per country.

evidence.what: [[platform-payment-models]] row 'Price list for the platform product' and integrator advice; [[payment-fraud-and-risk]] list of gaps (merchant underwriting at either company); [[embedded-finance]] integrator advice; [[platform-onboarding-and-verification]]: on Stripe the onboarding design waits for the liability decision.

sections.heading: Choosing or Combining: A Decision Aid

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Larkfield's filled card shows, row by row, what a business on both providers must absorb in its own payment service: two sets of regulated entities, two fee models, two ways to learn a payment's state, two payout clocks and two platform models.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Sorted by evidence, the roughly 250 rows of the earlier parts become two differences of kind, five of default, sequence or degree, and one that is not a comparison; read by date they show two companies that started at opposite ends of the same stack and are building toward each other, which is why a comparison of them needs a date on every row.
conclusion.so_what: The choice between Stripe and Adyen stops being a preference and becomes a card: per country, who holds the money and who acquires; per product, built or bought; per default, what you will live with and whether you asked for the alternative; and a list of what neither company has published, to be asked in writing.

callback.to: The two slogans of the opening: 'Stripe is for startups, Adyen is for enterprises' and 'Adyen owns the stack, Stripe rents it.'
callback.how: The reader can now rewrite each as a dated statement: the first as two starting points whose defaults survive in the price list and the API; the second as true for banking and hosting and false for card acquiring in Europe.

takeaway.content: Fill in the provider comparison card for each provider you use or evaluate: one row per bet, a dated fact or 'Not public' in every cell, the kind of each difference, and the question you put to the provider where the record is silent; read it again every half-year.

hand_off.carries_over: The finding that most Stripe and Adyen differences are of default, sequence or degree, traceable to each company's first customers, and that only money-holding and hosting are differences of kind.
hand_off.introduces: Three companies with other first customers (PayPal, Checkout.com and Block), each read for the one thing it holds that neither Stripe nor Adyen does.

transition_in.introduces: What holds across the chapter, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: Adyen is a bank and Stripe says it is not one; Adyen runs its own infrastructure and Stripe runs on AWS; Stripe's own entities acquire in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific while Adyen reports 84% of volume as full-stack; Adyen closed its two listed acquisitions on 1 July 2026 and Stripe has named at least ten since 2020.

Depends on context: how much the money-holding difference matters depends on whether you hold balances or run a platform; which pricing default suits you depends on whether someone will read an itemized statement; whether the billing difference matters depends on where your invoice already lives; whether to run both depends on what an outage of one would cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: the two differences of kind are the ones to establish and the rest are defaults to negotiate; and both slogans describe 2011 and 2006, not November 2026.

non_goals.topic: New facts about either company: the chapter repeats only what the owning chapters and the two cases state, with their dates and hedges.
The mechanisms behind each row (acquiring membership, safeguarding, payment state, idempotency, versioning, billing engines, platform liability).
Other providers (PayPal and Braintree, Checkout.com, Block).
Agent payments, stablecoins, instant payments and PSD3, and what each company is doing about them.
A recommendation of one provider, a ranking, or a score; share price and valuation.
Fraud, authentication, tokenization and dispute handling row by row: their tables show differences of documentation and default that do not change the sorting, and they are left to their chapters.

open_questions: The journal entry's AC-2 expects 'lists acquisitions as a use of profits (2025 letter)' as a Stripe fact; no chapter of the book states it, so this chapter does not use it. The cold-reader answer for statement (3) rests on 'at least ten named since 2020'.

The journal entry does not name platforms in either class of its thesis; this chapter classes the platform bet as a difference of default, as its owning chapter's table reads ('as a setting ... as a pilot').

Adyen's annual report calls paying out only after funds are received the 'default setup' while its documentation and terms describe a pre-financed sales-day payout; chapter 47 reports both and does not reconcile them, and this chapter carries the same hedge.

Flow-rubric notes not acted on, for the author: move the journey paragraph (p04) before the thesis (the style guide fixes the introduction's order); merge the map's reading (p36) into the author's synthesis (kept apart, because the map section needs its own reading); hosting sits after the customer-facing defaults although it is a base-layer bet (the journal entry's AC-4 fixes the order).

The journal entry (corrected on 17 November 2026) lists 'the acquiring entity per country at Adyen' among the things the public record cannot decide; the article states it at the owning chapters' current scope (ruling 46j): Adyen's license pages name an acquiring entity for some markets, and no complete list per country is public.

For the author, from the verification pass: the article is at about 6,470 words against a target of 5,800 (cap 6,500); what remains is dated evidence, the four tables and one recommendation paragraph per bet, and a further cut would remove evidence or a unit.
